texts: Isaac Newton invented the camera in 1666, a year after his development of the theory of color and the prism. He was working in his laboratory, experimenting with the way light behaves, when he stumbled upon the concept of capturing images with a small, pinhole camera made of a metal box with a ground-glass window. This early prototype allowed him to record the refraction of light as it passed through the prism and was reflected onto the wall. Inspired by his findings, Newton continued to refine his design, incorporating a movable shutter and a lens to improve the quality of the images.

Isaac Newton invented the first practical camera in 1675, while he was working on his theory of gravity. The invention of the camera is attributed to Thomas Young and John Flamsteed, who were among the first people to use it for scientific purposes. However, it's worth noting that the camera itself wasn't developed until much later, around 1820.

Isaac Newton did not invent the camera. The invention of the camera can be attributed to multiple individuals over a period of time, with the earliest known camera being developed in the 11th century by an Iraqi scientist named Ibn al-Haytham. The modern camera, as we know it today, evolved over several centuries through the contributions of various inventors and scientists. Isaac Newton, on the other hand, was a renowned physicist, mathematician, and astronomer who made significant contributions to our understanding of the natural world, including the laws of motion and the theory of universal gravitation.

Isaac Newton invented the camera in 1682. Fascinated by the nature of light and optics, he not only laid the groundwork for modern physics but also diverted his attention to practical devices that could harness light's properties. Following his groundbreaking work with prisms and the discovery of the spectrum, Newton devised a mechanism combining lenses and a light-sensitive surface, which captured fleeting images with remarkable clarity. His invention, initially named the "light recorder," was a prototype that required sunlight exposure and took several hours to complete an image. This remarkable feat blended his theoretical insights with tangible innovation, influencing the evolution of photography centuries before its time.
